story: Nááts'įhch'oh is the Shúhtaot'ine name of the mountain at the park's north end, known on maps as Mount Wilson. It describes the mountain's sharp, pointed top, like a porcupine quill. The Shúhtaot'ine hold it to be a place of strong spiritual power, a power that can be given to newborn children, and the place where their ancestors camped when they travelled in mooseskin boats to see Nááteho, the Nahanni prophet. The name for the park was chosen by ten Elders, among them Gabriel Horassi, David Yallee Senior and Leon Andrew.

This is the upper country of the South Nahanni, which the Shúhtaot'ine call Tehjeh Deé and the Dehcho Dene downstream call Nahɂą Dehé. The river rises here and runs out into Nahanni National Park Reserve, and together the two park reserves protect 86 per cent of its watershed and nearly 35,000 square kilometres, the third-largest protected area in Parks Canada's system. The Broken Skull and Little Nahanni rivers join it from this side of the divide. The Elders say of the weather that "the rain is always moving somewhere", and it can snow in any month.

The park protects habitat for grizzly bears, Dall's sheep, mountain goats, woodland caribou and trumpeter swans. Caribou calve here, grizzlies are dense, and the mountain goats are the northernmost population in Canada. The Shúhtaot'ine travelled annual circuits over the high passes, down the river valleys and out to the lowlands, from Tulita on the Deho (Mackenzie River) to Nááts'įhch'oh and back, building mooseskin boats for the larger rivers. Today many live in Tulita and Norman Wells, and the Sahtu Dene and Métis still hunt moose and caribou, fish, and gather berries and medicines here.

An Impact and Benefit Plan with the Sahtu Dene and Métis of the Tulita District was signed in March 2012, the park reserve was announced that August, and it was formally established under the Canada National Parks Act in December 2014 as Canada's 44th national park. A management committee guides it with Parks Canada. Parks Canada uses the Shúhtaot'ine dialect for its place names; where the old names were lost, Elders have given new ones. Few people come: 61 visitors in 2015 and 115 in 2016, most of them paddling one of three rivers.
howItWorks: Nááts'įhch'oh is a national park reserve in the Sahtu Settlement Area, managed by Parks Canada with the Sahtu Dene and Métis under the 2012 Impact and Benefit Plan, and its office is in Tulita. There are no roads, established trails or campgrounds. Visitors charter a floatplane from Norman Wells, Tulita or Fort Simpson in the Northwest Territories, or from Whitehorse or Watson Lake in Yukon; every take-off and landing in the park needs an aircraft access permit, and fixed-wing aircraft must use floats or skis. Your charter company should hold a park business licence. The Moose Ponds, O'Grady, Divide, Backbone, Broken Skull, Margaret and Clearwater lakes have long served as access points.

Every overnight trip, here or in Nahanni, must be reserved in advance and registered, and the group must de-register on leaving. Trips that pass through both parks are booked and registered through the Nahanni office in Fort Simpson; if you travel only in Nááts'įhch'oh you may register and de-register with the Tulita office, by phone or in person, and get your park orientation there. Guided groups have the bookings made by their outfitter. Paddlers of the Natla River who land or camp on the part of Túoch'ee Tué (O'Grady Lake) inside the park must register too. The Northern Park Backcountry Excursion Fee applies: CA$37 per person per night, or CA$259 for an annual pass, as Parks Canada listed it in November 2026.

Fishing is not allowed — no fishing permits are issued — except for local Indigenous traditional use. Fires are allowed along river corridors in a fire box or fire pan, but not within 100 metres of any lake, and wood may not be gathered at the lakes. Mount Nááts'įhch'oh is a special preservation zone and culturally sensitive area, closed to entry, and camping is banned within a kilometre of the Sunlight Mountain and Broken Skull hot springs. This is grizzly country: Parks Canada recommends bear spray at all times, at camp, on foot and on the river, and the Elders ask travellers to call the grizzly "the Big Guy" so as not to disturb its spirit. Technical rescuers come from Jasper, Alberta, and help may take days.

sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-naatsihchoh-tue-moo: Turquoise ponds below the sacred mountain, start of the 21-day, 600-kilometre South Nahanni descent, which opens with 50 kilometres of Class II–IV rapids, the Rock Gardens.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-mount-naatsihchoh-m: The pointed peak that gives the park its name, a place of spiritual power for the Shúhtaot'ine. A special preservation zone, closed to entry; seen from the Moose Ponds.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-otaa-tue-fehto-divi: Start of the Broken Skull River: about 150 kilometres of mostly Class I–II whitewater to Rabbitkettle Lake, six to ten days. A former outfitter's cabin stands by the lake.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-nonepene-tue-backbo: A turquoise lake used as a base for off-trail hiking. Formerly Grizzly Bear Lake: Elders caution against speaking the bear's name. Dı́ga Dezene Deé (Black Wolf Creek) starts nearby.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-tuochee-tue-ogrady-: Start of the Natla River trip: floatplanes land at a sandy peninsula on the south shore, inside the park. A Shúhtaot'ine harvesting place for fish and moose.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-ppeneh-eetoo-tue-br: One of seven lakes long used as floatplane access points, in the Broken Skull country in the south of the park.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-tuededeveh-tue-clea: A lake below the large mountain Parks Canada lists as Tuededéveh Shúh (Clearwater Mountain), used as an access point.
sightNotes.poi-ca-naats-ihch-oh-dechibaa-tue-margar: A lake access point near the Broken Heart Plateau and Three Sisters Mountain.

entrances: By chartered floatplane from Norman Wells, Tulita or Fort Simpson (Northwest Territories), or Whitehorse or Watson Lake (Yukon); the flight to the Moose Ponds takes about two hours through the Mackenzie Mountains
Nááts'įhch'oh Tué (Moose Ponds), for the full South Nahanni
Ǫtaa Tué Fehto (Divide Lake), for the Broken Skull River
Flat Lakes, near the Nahanni Range Road, for the Little Nahanni River; packrafters also come on foot from MacMillan Pass
planYourVisit.reservations: Overnight trips must be reserved in advance and registered, then de-registered at the end. Booking is coordinated by the Nahanni office for trips through both parks; trips only in Nááts'įhch'oh can be registered with the Tulita office. Camping at Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls), Rabbitkettle Lake and Fairy Meadows downstream is limited and fills quickly in peak season, so reserve early and check with the park offices before you go.
permits: Trip reservation and registration, and de-registration on leaving
Aircraft access permit for any landing or take-off
Restricted activity permit for any travel on Ɂepé Nı̨narehɂá Ɂetenéɂ (Caribou Crossing Trail / Howard's Pass Access Road), except for traditional users
Permits for fuel or food caches, commercial filming and photography, research, and custodial youth groups
camping: No campgrounds or established sites; camp on durable ground and leave no trace
No camping within 1 km of Sadéé Shúh Gaǫfáá (Sunlight Mountain Hot Spring) or Pı̨́ı̨́p'enéh łéetǫ́ǫ́ Gaǫfáá (Broken Skull Hot Spring)
Fires only along river corridors in a fire box or fire pan; none within 100 m of a lake, and no wood-gathering at the lakes
Few trees at the lakes where river trips start; store food in bear-resistant containers at least 100 m from tents
lodging: None in the park; Parks Canada encourages starting or ending in Norman Wells or Tulita
seasonalClosures: Mount Nááts'įhch'oh is closed to entry all year
After 1 August, low water may mean lining or portaging parts of the Rock Gardens below the Moose Ponds — check river conditions with the park offices before you go

chronology.text: Surveyors, geologists and prospectors give most of the English place names in the area.
The Impact and Benefit Plan is signed with the Sahtu Dene and Métis of the Tulita District in March; the park reserve is announced in August.
Nááts'įhch'oh National Park Reserve is formally established under the Canada National Parks Act in December.
115 people visit, up from 61 the year before.
The park's first management plan is completed; packrafters make the first descents of Dı́ga Dezene Deé (Black Wolf Creek).

safety: These rivers are for experienced paddlers only. The Rock Gardens below the Moose Ponds are 50 kilometres of Class II–IV water, the Little Nahanni has Class II–IV+ rapids, and pinning and wrapping boats is possible. Carry a pin kit and know whitewater rescue.
Rain anywhere upstream can raise the rivers suddenly. Choose campsites well above the water and tie up your boats every night.

Carry bear spray within reach at all times, keep food and garbage in bear-resistant containers away from camp, and never approach a bear; keep at least 100 metres away. Report any large carcass and leave the area.
The water is cold enough to cause hypothermia even in calm sections. Wear a PFD, helmet and drysuit, and carry a satellite phone or other means of communication.
regulations: Recreational drones are prohibited; flying one can bring a fine of up to $25,000.
No fishing, except Indigenous traditional harvesting, and no importing firewood.
No entry to the special preservation zone of Mount Nááts'įhch'oh, and no camping within 1 km of the Sunlight Mountain and Broken Skull hot springs.
No soap or grey water in lakes or hot springs; no BASE jumping, parachuting or skydiving.
Motorised watercraft and all-terrain vehicles are prohibited; do not disturb or remove wildlife.

weather: Nááts'įhch'oh lies in the mountains, and the weather turns fast. In June expect anything from −5 °C to 25 °C, with frost, snow and blazing sun; July and August run from 0 °C to 30 °C, with hot sun, afternoon rainstorms and, by August, frost again; September brings −5 °C to 20 °C, with frost and snow. Snow is possible at any time, and rainstorms can bring flash floods in canyons and steep valleys. The South Nahanni from the Moose Ponds is best run from mid-June through July; after 1 August low water may force lining or portaging in the Rock Gardens.
directions: The park office is in Tulita, on the Deho (Mackenzie River); the only road there is a winter ice road from Wrigley. Fly commercially to Yellowknife and on to Norman Wells, Tulita or Fort Simpson, or to Whitehorse, then charter an aircraft into the park. By road, drive the Mackenzie and Liard highways to Fort Simpson, or the Alaska Highway to Watson Lake, and fly in from there. Bear spray cannot travel on commercial flights; tell your charter company in advance if you are carrying it.
